claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution with uniformly distributed Mg.
Service-relevant high-temperature exposure promotes diffusion-controlled phase separation in Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Diffusion-driven Mg segregation initiates the nucleation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates grow and coalesce during continued thermal exposure.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates preferentially develop along grain boundaries.
The evolving intermetallic precipitates disrupt the continuity of the metastable solid solution.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation compromises the uniformity and formation of the protective passive film.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates establish local galvanic cells.
Intermetallic-induced passive-film disruption and galvanic coupling accelerate localized corrosion.
Intermetallic-induced passive-film disruption and galvanic coupling accelerate oxidation reactions.
High-temperature exposure will increase the fraction and coarseness of Mg-containing intermetallic phases in the matrix and along grain boundaries relative to the initial state.
High-temperature exposure will reduce corrosion resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
High-temperature exposure will deteriorate oxidation performance relative to the initial metastable state.
The homogeneous initial metastable solid-solution state has superior corrosion resistance.
The homogeneous initial metastable solid-solution state has superior high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Above a critical service temperature, Mg diffusion and intermetallic precipitation become significant.
At lower temperatures, Mg diffusion and intermetallic precipitation are kinetically suppressed.
